Let me ask you something. Have you ever had a completely normal day... and then opened your phone... and suddenly felt like your life wasn't good enough? Nothing actually happened. Your life didn't get worse. You didn't lose anything. Five minutes earlier... you were fine. Then you see someone traveling. Someone bought a new car. Someone started a business. Someone got married. Someone moved to another country. Someone your age is doing something you've been dreaming about for years. And suddenly... your own life feels smaller. You start thinking... “Why am I not there yet?” “What am I doing with my life?” “Everyone is moving forward.” “I'm the only one falling behind.” But here's the strange part. You don't actually know if their life is better than yours. You just know... their life looks better from where you're standing. And those are two completely different things. Because your brain has a very dangerous habit. It takes a tiny piece of someone else's life... and compares it to the entire story of your own. And once you understand how that happens... you'll start seeing your life very differently.

Think about the last time you opened Instagram... or YouTube... or TikTok... and started scrolling without really thinking. One person is traveling. Another is making money. Another is getting fit. Another is building a company. Another is living alone in some beautiful apartment. Another is constantly surrounded by friends. Another seems incredibly confident. And after ten minutes... you've watched dozens of people living what looks like... a better life than yours. But there's something you never see. The boring Tuesday. The bad morning. The failed plan. The argument. The uncertainty. The rejection. The loneliness. The doubt. The things they don't post. You don't see those. You see the result. You see the photograph. You see the announcement. You see the achievement. You see the five seconds worth showing. And then you compare it... to the parts of your life that nobody sees. That's not a fair comparison. But your brain doesn't care. It still makes the comparison.

And this is where social media gets interesting. Because human beings have always compared themselves to other people. You don't need the internet for that. Thousands of years ago... you could look at the person next to you... and wonder if they were stronger. More respected. More successful. More attractive. More capable. Comparison helped humans understand where they stood inside a group. But there was one major limitation. You could only compare yourself to the people around you. Maybe a few dozen people. Maybe a few hundred. Today... you can compare yourself to millions. Before breakfast. Without leaving your bed. You can see the richest people... the most successful people... the most talented people... the most adventurous people... the most productive people... all in the same five minutes. And your brain doesn't process that as... “Here are millions of unusual examples.” It can start feeling like... “This is what everyone is doing.” And that's the illusion.

Imagine you're standing in a room... and there are one hundred people. Ninety-five of them are having completely ordinary days. Five are having something exciting happen. Maybe someone got a promotion. Someone traveled somewhere beautiful. Someone launched a business. Someone got engaged. Now imagine that you had a camera... but you could only film those five people. After watching the footage... what would you think everyone in the room was doing? You'd probably think... everyone was living an extraordinary life. But the camera didn't show reality. It showed a selection of reality. That's basically what happens online. The internet isn't showing you life. It's showing you... what people decided was worth showing.

And there's another problem. You don't compare yourself to random people. You compare yourself to people who are ahead of you... in the exact area you're insecure about. If you're worried about money... you suddenly notice people making more money. If you're worried about your career... you notice people getting promoted. If you're worried about your social life... you notice people surrounded by friends. If you're worried about your future... you notice people who seem to have everything figured out. Your brain becomes a search engine... for evidence that you're behind. And once it starts looking... it finds plenty. That's why comparison can become addictive. Not because you actually want another person's life. But because your brain keeps asking... “How do I measure up?” And there is no final answer. Because there will always be someone ahead. Someone younger. Someone richer. Someone more experienced. Someone more talented. Someone who started earlier. Someone who got lucky. Someone who had opportunities you didn't have. You can achieve something you've wanted for years... and five minutes later... you can find someone who has achieved ten times more. And suddenly... your achievement feels ordinary. This is how the finish line keeps moving.

You get the job... then you want the better job. You reach a goal... then you find someone who reached it faster. You buy something you've wanted... then you see someone with something better. You make progress... then you discover someone who is further ahead. And if you keep using other people as your scoreboard... there is no point at which you can finally say... “I'm doing enough.” Because the scoreboard keeps changing. And this is where something even deeper happens. You can start wanting things... not because you actually want them... but because other people have them. You see someone traveling... and suddenly you want to travel. You see someone building a business... and suddenly you feel like you should build one. You see someone waking up at five in the morning... and suddenly you feel guilty for sleeping. You see someone reading fifty books a year... and suddenly your own pace feels embarrassing. You see someone who seems completely certain about their future... and suddenly you're questioning yours. But ask yourself something. If nobody could see your life... would you still want all of these things? That's a difficult question. Because sometimes... we aren't chasing a better life. We're chasing a life... that looks better from the outside. And those aren't always the same thing.

Imagine you could press a button... and nobody would ever see your achievements. No Instagram. No followers. No likes. No one to impress. Nobody would know how much money you make. Nobody would know what car you drive. Nobody would know where you travel. Nobody would know how productive you are. Nobody would know what you've accomplished. You would still have your life... but there would be no audience. What would you actually choose? What would you still work toward? What would still matter to you? That question can reveal something important. Because maybe some of the things you're chasing... aren't actually your goals. Maybe they're borrowed goals. And there's nothing wrong with wanting success. There's nothing wrong with wanting money. There's nothing wrong with wanting a better career... or a better life. The problem isn't ambition. The problem is... letting someone else's life decide what your life should look like.

Because here's something we forget. You don't see people's starting points. You see their current position. You don't know what opportunities they had. You don't know who helped them. You don't know what they sacrificed. You don't know how long they've been working. You don't know what happened behind the scenes. And you definitely don't know what their life feels like from the inside. Two people can have completely different lives... and the person who looks more successful from the outside... might not feel more fulfilled on the inside. You simply don't have enough information to know. But your brain still creates a story. And that story usually sounds something like this: “They're doing better.” “I'm behind.” “They figured it out.” “I haven't.” “They're moving forward.” “I'm stuck.” And after hearing that story enough times... you start believing it. Not because it's true. Because you've repeated it.

And this is why comparison can become dangerous. It doesn't just make you feel bad. It can change what you do. You stop enjoying your progress... because you're too busy measuring it. You stop working on your goals... because someone else is already ahead. You stop appreciating your life... because you're constantly looking at someone else's. And sometimes... you abandon something you genuinely cared about... just because it doesn't look impressive enough. Imagine two people learning the same skill. The first person improves slowly... but enjoys the process. The second person improves slowly... but constantly checks how everyone else is doing. Same progress. Completely different experience. The first person thinks... “I'm getting better.” The second thinks... “I'm still behind.” The difference isn't necessarily their life. It's the scoreboard they're using.

So what do you do about it? You don't need to delete every social media app. You don't need to stop caring about success. And you don't need to convince yourself that comparison doesn't exist. That's unrealistic. The goal is not to never compare. The goal is to notice... when comparison has started controlling you. The next time you see someone and immediately think... “I'm behind.” Pause. And ask... “Behind according to who?” That's it. Behind according to who? Who decided that you should already be there? Who decided your timeline was supposed to look like theirs? Who decided that your life had to follow the same sequence? Because sometimes... you're not actually behind. You're simply on a different path.

And there's another question that's even more useful. Instead of asking... “Am I doing better than them?” ask... “Am I doing better than I was?” That's a completely different game. Because now... your past self becomes the reference point. Did you learn something? Did you become more disciplined? Did you make one difficult decision? Did you get better at something? Did you understand yourself a little more? Did you keep going when it would've been easier to quit? Those things might not look impressive online. But they're real. And here's the weird thing about real progress. Most of it is invisible. Nobody sees you choosing not to waste an hour. Nobody sees you practicing when you're bad at something. Nobody sees you studying when you're tired. Nobody sees you keeping a promise you made to yourself. Nobody sees the small decisions... that slowly change your life. But those decisions still count. Even when there is no audience. Because your life isn't a performance. It's the thing happening... when nobody is watching.

So maybe the goal isn't to build a life... that looks better than everyone else's. Maybe the goal is to build a life... that actually feels like yours. A life you don't constantly need to escape from. A life where your goals make sense to you. A life where you're proud of the direction... even if you're not at the destination yet. And that changes the question completely. Instead of... “Why is everyone doing better than me?” you start asking... “What kind of life do I actually want?” Instead of... “Why am I so far behind?” you ask... “What's the next step for me?” Instead of... “Why don't I have what they have?” you ask... “Do I even want what they have?” And instead of... “Am I winning?” you ask... “Am I becoming someone I respect?” Because maybe... the biggest problem isn't that everyone else is living better than you. Maybe the problem... is that you're constantly looking at everyone else... instead of looking at your own life. The next time you open your phone... and suddenly feel like you're behind... remember this. You're seeing someone's highlight... not their entire life. You're seeing their outcome... not their process. You're seeing what they chose to show... not everything they had to go through. And you're comparing that tiny window... to everything you know about yourself. Of course the comparison feels unfair. It is. So don't let someone else's highlight reel... turn your ordinary Tuesday... into something you hate. Don't let another person's timeline... convince you that yours is wrong. Don't let someone else's definition of success... become your definition of failure. You don't need to win someone else's life. You need to build your own. And maybe... for the first time... that's enough. Think deeper. Live better. Become more. This is Why We Become.
